Figure III-3 also shows the implied levels of non-Crow income. The baseline condition with no other Crow coal development (AF-1) shows non-Crow income rising from about $10 million in 1975 to $15 million by the year 2000. If no other significant Crow coal development occurs, West-moreland Resources' most probable level of development makes only about a $1.5 million addition to this total since only a relatively small part of the increased Westmoreland employment is filled by non-Crows. With other significant Crow coal development (AF-2) however, the situation is quite a bit different. The baseline moves gradually from about $10 to $18 million, but the incremental impact of Westmoreland Resources' low level production (Scenario 1) on non-Crow income is more than $4 million through the mid 1980's, falling to about $2 million during the remainder of the period.
Figure III-4 shows what is likely to happen to non-agricultural per capita labor income in the impact area. For the Crows, the impact of Westmoreland's most probable level of production (Scenario 1) is substantial under either development level, but their assumed rapid population growth (discussed under Community Impacts) may eventually cause declines in per capita income under either projected level of Crow coal development. With other significant Crow coal development, however, the decline does not become serious until 1990. By then there may be an adjustment in birth rates or increased out-migration may occur.
The same pattern was not obtained for the non-Crows in the impact area. Their per capita income changes in much the same way as total income and employment, because their assumed rate of population increase is more modest and out-migration is likely to be less.
